source.title: Beyond Surface Alignment: Rebuilding LLMs Safety Mechanism via Probabilistically Ablating Refusal Direction
source.authors: Yuanbo Xie; Yingji Zhang; Tian-Yun Liu; Duo-He Ma; Ting-Wen Liu

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates whether prefilling and refusal-direction attacks bypass safety, and whether training with probabilistic activation ablation improves robustness. These tests bear on the claims but are not reproductions of the original studies' methods.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior work for per-token KL concentration and harmful fine-tuning; those cited results are not this study's results. Its own measurements include a prefilling-length experiment, refusal-direction attack evaluations, and a refusal-direction activation measurement.
record.test_reason: Its own results bear on V4 (prefilling and GCG suffix attacks on aligned models, Fig. 2 and Table 1). They also bear on V7: harmful-prefix augmentation, i.e. Qi et al.'s deepening data, and DeepRefusal, tested against prefilling and other attacks in Tables 1, 3, 4 and 6. The method differs from the originals, and no per-token KL is measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say existing defenses, including Qi et al.'s augmentation and CircuitBreaker, are surface-level and are bypassed by refusal-direction and transfer attacks. DeepRefusal, which ablates the refusal direction across layers and token depths plus prefix augmentation, cuts ASR by about 95% across four models and six attacks with small capability loss. Over-refusal is not significantly increased at p=0.5, and rises only at large p.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes fine-tuning with probabilistic activation ablation across layers and token positions, together with harmful-prefix augmentation; it does not reproduce either original study's method.
record.method_sensitivity: Prefilled content length changes attack success. PAA probability changes attack success and over-refusal; the authors identify p=0.5 as the best balance. Removing harmful-prefix augmentation worsens prefilling robustness. Results also vary by attack construction and model.

fits_no_version.finding: Under adversarial prompts, cosine similarity between last-token activations and the refusal direction declines.
Refusal-direction ablation attacks reach 90-92% ASR on instruction-tuned models and transfer to refusal-trained variants (Table 1, Table 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation-level refusal-direction attacks bypass safety training, including token-deepened training.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The prefilling-length result in Figure 2 is presented as a figure without numerical values in the text. The paper notes that model size, architecture, and training data can affect performance, and that high-quality data to mitigate over-refusal is important. The PAA probability sweep reports increased over-refusal at high probability.
record.rows_left_out: Other attack types, models, languages, and capability benchmark results were not extracted because the selected rows capture the tested claim versions and their main conditions. Table 1 and Appendix C report additional attack/model/language comparisons.

untested.parts: No harmful fine-tuning; the authors put fine-tuning attacks out of scope.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models. The first-token concentration is only cited from Qi et al.
Decoding changes are not tested. Suffixes are tested only via GCG in Table 1, which no row records.
Refusal-direction work concerns a representation direction, not a small set of weights or ranks.
No test of whether the data or objective causes shallowness.
Safety is not measured as a function of response position, and fine-tuning attacks on deepened models are not tested.

missing.what: Prefilling ASR of unmodified instruct models: Llama3 86.8, Llama2 30.1, Gemma 17.5 (Mistral row unreadable)
GCG suffix ASR on unmodified instruct models (Llama3 24.0, Llama2 34.0, Gemma 46.0)
RT-Augmented (Qi et al. deepening) ASR across all attacks and four models: prefilling low (Llama3 3.0, Gemma 0.2) but Refusal/Refusal-Transfer high
DeepRefusal prefilling and other ASRs on Llama2, Mistral and Gemma, including Llama2 Refusal 36.9
Capability cost of deepening: DeepRefusal MT-bench 5.94 vs 6.89, GSM8k 72.40 vs 75.44 on Llama3; RT-Augmented values
Over-refusal of RT-Augmented vs DeepRefusal across models

record.verdict_notes: The Table 1 text is garbled for Mistral (rows have 6 of 7 values), so Mistral values are left unread. Tables 3 and 4 disagree slightly for the default p=0.5 model (prefilling 0.4 vs 0.0; Refusal 0.2 vs 3.3). The ablations suggest token-depth robustness to prefilling comes from Qi-style harmful-prefix augmentation, not from PAA (R3 vs R10). The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test harmful fine-tuning with a few to a few hundred harmful examples as a safety-compromising intervention.
The study does not test ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning as an intervention that raises harmful compliance.
It does not measure per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models or test whether KL is concentrated in the first response positions.
The study tests prefilling and refusal-direction attacks, but not adversarial suffixes or decoding changes.
It does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
It does not establish that the training data or objective causes safety shallowness.

The study evaluates a training method designed to extend robustness across token and layer depths, including under prefilling and other attacks, but does not measure safety as a function of response position.

rows.subject: Llama3-8B-instruct
rows.operation_detail: Increase the length of prefilled harmful tokens.
rows.note: The text says attack success rate rises significantly as prefilled content length increases; numerical values are only shown in the figure.
rows.check: Figure 2's text does not name the model. 'Llama3-8B-instruct' is the reader's assumption. Values are figure-only; the text says ASR 'rises significantly' with prefill length.

rows.subject: Llama3-8B-instruct(+RT)
rows.note: The table reports this refusal-training comparator before the PAA probability sweep.
rows.check: Refusal training alone is not a deepening method, so drop V7. Its prefilling ASR of 82.7 bears on V4. The unmodified Llama3-8B-instruct value in Table 1 is 86.8; that row is missing.

rows.subject: Llama3-8B-instruct +DeepRefusal(p=0)
rows.stage_stated: instruct; fine-tuned with DeepRefusal configuration at p=0
rows.operation_detail: Use DeepRefusal training with PAA probability p=0.
rows.note: The table's p=0 setting still includes the other DeepRefusal training components.
rows.check: p=0 removes PAA but keeps harmful-prefix augmentation. Its numbers match the RT-Augmented row of Table 1 exactly (Qi et al.-style deepening). Prefilling ASR 3.0 vs 82.7 for RT. This is a defense result, so drop V4.

source_check.locator_found: Table 4: p=0, PrefillingAttack; RT baseline. Table 1: matching RT-Augmented result.

rows.check: Drop V4. Table 4 gives prefilling 0.0 for p=0.5, but Table 3 gives 0.4 for the same default DeepRefusal. Refusal-attack ASR also differs: 3.3 in Table 4 vs 0.2 in Table 3.

rows.subject: Llama3-8B-instruct +DeepRefusal(p=1)

rows.subject: Llama3-8B-instruct +DeepRefusal(p=1)
rows.note: The authors state that large p values cause excessive over-refusal.
rows.check: This is a cost measure (over-refusal), not the deepening effect itself. At p=0.5, over-refusal is 28.5, below RT's 39.5; only large p exceeds RT.
